description:
EarthScope presents a NASA Earth science data exploration platform designed by an experienced to investigate environmental trends using satellite observations and scientific model outputs.

This platform will allow users to not only explore how environmental variables change over time but also identify regional differences, measure the magnitude and direction of trends, and evaluate their statistical significance.
summary: Every year some place is called the hottest, greenest or driest ever, but one record year proves nothing. EarthScope is a web app that tells you, for any place on Earth, whether a change in NASA data is real or just natural ups and downs. It reads three NASA records: GISTEMP temperature (1980 to 2025), MODIS vegetation (2010 to 2025) and GPM IMERG rainfall (2010 to 2024). For each one it measures the change per decade and tests it against that place’s own year-to-year swings. On maps it corrects for testing thousands of places at once, so chance results fade out. Trend Detective puts two records side by side to expose hidden causes. Our clearest case is Punjab, Pakistan: farmland got about 13% greener from 2010 to 2025 (p < 0.001) while rainfall showed no trend, which points to irrigation from groundwater. EarthScope also gives ten-year outlooks as tested ranges, shows the IPCC’s projections to 2100, and answers plain questions like “Is Punjab getting greener?”. It is live at earthscope.us.
details:
EarthScope

EarthScope: the Earth over South Asia, coloured by NASA vegetation data

How this started

There are five of us, all from Lahore: Muhammad Hadi, Mohammed Ahmed, Ch Ahmed Mubashar, Muhammad Shehroz and Ibrahim. This project really started with a complaint. It was the middle of November and it still felt like summer, and someone said what we all hear every year, that this is the hottest year ever. Then someone else asked the obvious question. Is it actually getting worse, or does it just feel that way because it is hot today? None of us could answer properly, and that bothered us more than the heat.

When we read the "Be an Earth System Trend Detective" challenge, it was basically our argument written down as a brief. Show what is changing on Earth, where, how fast, and whether a scientist would call it real. So that is what we tried to build: a tool that tells you, for any place on the planet, whether a change is real or just the normal ups and downs of weather.

We also knew who we wanted it to be for. NASA's data is free, but using it is hard. You have to download huge files, write code, and understand statistics that most people never learn. The people who most need a straight answer, like someone running a district's water supply, a teacher, or a reporter checking a headline before it goes out, usually can't do any of that. We wanted them to get the answer in seconds.

Where to find everything

  • Project site: earthscope.us
  • The app: earthscope.us/app
  • 3D studio: earthscope.us/3d
  • Research paper: EarthScope_Paper.pdf
  • Project report: EarthScope_Report.pdf
  • Business model: EarthScope_Business_Model.pdf
  • Code: GitHub
  • Video: YouTube
  • Proof of Work (our files from the weekend): Google Drive

It is all free. There is no login, we don't collect anyone's data, and it works on a phone.

What EarthScope does

What EarthScope does: see the change, test it, look ahead

The app

When you open the app you land on a 3D globe wrapped in NASA's Blue Marble imagery. If you tick "Show trend columns", every place on Earth grows a little column, and the taller it is, the faster things are changing there. It is the quickest way we found to show someone the whole planet's story in one look. Under the globe there is the global temperature chart and a world map of trends.

The EarthScope app, exploring vegetation over the Indus plains

The part we spent the most time on is Explore. You click anywhere on the map, or pick a region like the Indus plains, and it builds a full report for that place:

  • the whole monthly record going back years, with the yearly averages on top
  • the trend line and the band around it that shows how sure we are
  • the change per decade as an actual number, and a verdict in plain words: high confidence, moderate, or likely noise
  • a ten-year forecast drawn as a widening band rather than a single line
  • a chart showing how our forecasts would have done in the past
  • a small table showing which forecasting models made the cut
  • for temperature, what the IPCC expects by 2100
  • a button to download the raw numbers

Compare lets you put two places side by side, say Punjab against the Nile delta, or Lahore against Karachi. Insights is where Trend Detective lives, which is the part that found our main result, and we explain it further down.

Then there is Ask EarthScope, which is honestly the part people enjoy most when we show them. It is a question box. You type something like "Is Punjab getting greener?" and it replies, "Yes, Punjab (Indus plains) is greening. Vegetation changed by +0.028 per decade from 2010 to 2025, about 13% higher than in 2010 to 2012," and marks it high confidence. If you ask "Did it rain more in Punjab?" it tells you rainfall barely moved and that normal year-to-year swings could easily explain it.

Ask EarthScope answering real questions with real numbers

It is not an AI chatbot. We wrote rules that pick out the place, the record and the time period from your question, and then it runs the exact same tests as the rest of the app, so it cannot invent a number. Because we are from Lahore, we taught it a few Roman Urdu words too, so barish, garmi and hariyali all work.

Who we picture using it

We kept a few real people in mind while building:

  • Someone in Punjab's irrigation department who opens the Indus plains and sees in ten seconds that the fields have been greening for years while rainfall hasn't changed. That tells them the extra water is coming from canals and tubewells.
  • A journalist who hears "Karachi has never been hotter" and wants to check before printing it.
  • A teacher in a government school who rotates the GRACE-FO satellites in front of the class and shows how a satellite can weigh water from space.
  • A student who will never read a chart but can type a question and get an answer.

The project site and the 3D models

We didn't want the method to be a wall of text, so the project site explains it with 3D scenes you can drag around. Everything 3D is built in code with three.js. None of it is video and none of it is AI-generated.

The scenes:

  • How a satellite measures plant health. Healthy leaves reflect a lot of near-infrared light and soak up red light, and the vegetation index we use is built from that difference.
  • How GRACE-FO weighs water. NASA's two GRACE-FO satellites fly one behind the other. When they pass over heavier ground, ground holding more water for example, the front satellite gets tugged slightly ahead, and that tiny change in the gap between them tells you how much water is down there. That one surprised a lot of our friends.
  • Punjab. A farming plain with crops on top and the water table underneath, with a slider that moves through the years so you can watch the fields get greener while the water level drops. We label it as an illustration, because it is one, and the real numbers are in the app.
  • One hot year. A simple scene showing why one hot year sitting on top of a long record doesn't prove anything.

Further down the page are the actual satellites behind our data, as 3D models with a card for each:

  • Terra launched in December 1999 and carries the MODIS instrument our vegetation data comes from.
  • Aqua launched in May 2002 with a second MODIS.
  • NOAA-20 launched in November 2017 and carries VIIRS, which is what will keep the vegetation record going once MODIS retires.
  • The GPM Core Observatory, a joint NASA and JAXA mission launched in February 2014, anchors the rainfall record.
  • GRACE-FO, from NASA and Germany's GFZ, launched in May 2018 and measures groundwater, which is the dataset we want to add next.

Each card says when the satellite went up, who built it, what instruments it carries and why we use it. The models aren't to scale. They only animate while they're on screen so the page stays fast on a phone, and if a phone can't do 3D the page still reads fine.

All of this is also in the 3D studio. You can save any scene as a 4K picture with a transparent background, record a short clip, or download a 3D model that PowerPoint can rotate during a talk. We made the visuals for our own video and slides this way, and a teacher could do the same.

The research paper

We also wrote a proper research paper. It walks through our question, the data, each method and why we picked it, every result with its uncertainty, our references, and where the work falls short.

The paper digs further into Punjab than the app does. Over the longer 2001 to 2025 vegetation record, monsoon rain actually did increase, so a lazy comparison could fool you. The paper pulls the two apart, and once rain's effect is taken out, the fields are still greening at about +0.024 per decade, with less than a one in a thousand chance that it's luck. So rain isn't the explanation.

We also wrote down what would prove us wrong. If NASA's GRACE-FO data showed groundwater under Punjab staying level while the fields got greener, our irrigation explanation would fall apart. We'd rather say that openly than hide it, and it's exactly the check we want to run next.

There is more on the site too. Our project report covers what we built and how to run it. The data analysis shows every number with the test behind it. The business model sets out who pays and our first year.

The data, and getting 36 GB down to something usable

Three NASA records on one 2 degree grid

On Thursday we downloaded about 36 GB of raw NASA files, covering three records:

  • Temperature comes from GISTEMP v4, made by NASA's Goddard Institute for Space Studies from weather stations on land plus ships and buoys at sea. We use it from 1980 to 2025, measured against the 1951 to 1980 average.
  • Vegetation comes from MODIS MOD13C2 on the Terra satellite, through NASA's Land Processes archive, from 2010 to 2025. It's a number called NDVI that runs from about zero for bare ground to about 0.9 for thick forest.
  • Rainfall comes from GPM IMERG, through NASA's GES DISC, from 2010 to 2024. It blends a fleet of satellites with rain gauges on the ground, and GPM is run jointly with Japan's space agency, JAXA.

You can't just open those three and compare them. They came at different resolutions, with MODIS at 0.05 degrees and IMERG at 0.1, in different units, and each one marked missing data its own way. So before we ran a single test we cleaned all of it:

  • Missing readings had been stored as fake numbers like -9999, which wreck any average, so we treated them as missing.
  • MODIS stores its values as whole numbers to save space, so we applied the scale factors to turn them back into real values.
  • We put rainfall into consistent monthly amounts.
  • Some files measured longitude from 0 to 360 and others from minus 180 to 180, and latitudes didn't all run the same way, so we lined all of that up.
  • We averaged everything onto one shared grid of 2 degree squares, 90 by 180 of them, with one value per month.

That took 36 GB down to about 160 MB, and every square now has temperature, vegetation and rain for the same place and the same months. That alignment is what makes the rest possible, especially comparing two records side by side. If someone wants to add another monthly NASA dataset later, it goes through the same steps.

How we decide whether a change is real: our models

The first thing we do is turn months into years. Monthly numbers carry the seasons and a lot of short-term memory, and both make trend tests look more certain than they should. So each place gets one average per calendar year, and a year only counts if at least nine of its months have good data. We also skip the current half-finished year, because a few hot months at the start of a year can drag a result around.

To decide whether there's a trend at all we use the Mann-Kendall test. It compares every year with every later year and counts how often the later one is higher. Because it only cares about the order of the values, one freak year can't create a trend that isn't there. On top of that we correct for the fact that a hot year tends to follow a hot year, using the method from Hamed and Rao (1998), because without that correction the test gets overconfident. It's the standard test in climate and water research, and it doesn't assume the data falls in a neat bell curve, which climate data usually doesn't.

For how fast things are changing we use Sen's slope. It works out the slope between every pair of years and takes the middle one, which means a single strange year can't pull it off course the way it would pull an ordinary straight line. We report it per decade, with a 95% range.

Maps have their own problem, and this is the part we're most proud of. If you test 1,481 patches of land and call anything under the usual 5% threshold a real change, around 74 of them will pass by pure luck. Most climate maps ignore that and colour them in anyway, and climate scientists have been complaining about it for years (Wilks wrote a well-known paper on it in 2016). We correct for it using the Benjamini-Hochberg method, which keeps the share of false alarms near 5%, and anything that doesn't survive gets faded out.

Before and after correcting for luck: 20.7% of land looks changed, 6.5% really is

The difference is big. For vegetation, 20.7% of the world's land looks like it changed if you test each place on its own. After the correction it's 6.5%, which is 5.9% greening and 0.6% browning.

We then turn all of this into one of three plain labels, high confidence, moderate or likely noise, because nobody outside a lab makes decisions based on a p-value.

For Punjab we went further. The province has two growing seasons. Kharif runs from May to October, during the monsoon, when rice, cotton and sugarcane grow. Rabi runs from November to April, the dry winter, when wheat grows. We tested each season on its own:

  • Kharif greened by about +0.031 per decade, from 0.349 to 0.391, with roughly a one in a thousand chance of being luck.
  • Rabi greened by about +0.028 per decade, from 0.362 to 0.400, with about a one in seventy-five chance.

The winter number is the one that convinced us. Wheat grows when there is almost no rain, so if the fields are getting greener then, the water has to be coming from somewhere else.

We also wanted to know when the change started, so we used the Pettitt test, which looks for the year a record shifted. Punjab's vegetation stepped up after 2018, from an average of 0.358 to 0.387. Global temperature stepped up after 2001, from +0.33 C to +0.81 C above the 1951 to 1980 average. Knowing the year matters if you're trying to tie a change to something real on the ground, like a new canal or a change in electricity subsidies for tubewells.

We tried to break our own Punjab result too. We dropped each year in turn and ran the test again. Every time, the result stayed far below the usual 5% line, so no single odd year is holding it up.

Punjab greening test with each year left out in turn: always far below p = 0.05

Forecasting the next ten years

We didn't want a forecast that just draws a confident line into the future, so we use five simple models and make each one prove itself first:

  • the average of the last ten years, which is the honest baseline
  • next year looks like last year
  • a straight-line trend
  • a sturdier version of the trend that ignores outliers
  • a trend that slowly eases off over time, known as damped Holt smoothing

Before any model counts, it has to forecast years it never saw, starting from lots of different points in the past. A model that can't beat the plain ten-year average gets dropped. The ones that survive get more weight the more accurate they were. The width of the forecast band comes from how wrong the models actually were in those tests, using a method called split-conformal intervals, so the uncertainty is earned rather than guessed.

How much better each forecasting model is than the ten-year average

Then we checked ourselves. For global temperature, the trend models beat the plain average by 27 to 45%, and each ends up carrying about a fifth to a quarter of the weight. Our 90% band caught the real value 78% of the time when we tested it on the past. That's short of the 90% it should be, and we thought about hiding it, but we decided to print it right next to the forecast instead. The 2035 outlook for global temperature is +1.30 C above the 1951 to 1980 average, somewhere between 0.91 and 1.68. For rainfall, the models barely beat the plain average, and the app says that too.

Global temperature since 1980 with the trend and the ten-year forecast range

A trend line can't see as far as 2100. That needs proper climate models, so for temperature we show the IPCC's latest global projections. By 2081 to 2100 they put warming at about 2.7 C above pre-industrial on the middle-road scenario (SSP2-4.5, somewhere between 2.1 and 3.5), and about 4.4 C if emissions stay high (SSP5-8.5, between 3.3 and 5.7). The app says plainly that these are world averages and not the specific place you clicked.

Trend Detective

Trend Detective is the idea that led to our main finding. It takes two records for the same place, say vegetation and rainfall, and flags it when they don't add up. If fields are getting greener but it isn't raining any more than before, something else is going on that neither chart would show you alone. The short summaries it writes are generated from the numbers each time, and we always word them as "consistent with" and never "caused by", because two things moving together isn't proof.

Checking our own work

We were nervous about getting the maths wrong, so we wrote the trend test twice, once in Python for the backend and once in JavaScript for the browser. On the same data they agree to seven decimal places, so a bug in one would show up as a mismatch. Every answer the website receives is also checked against a fixed format before it reaches a chart, so if something breaks you get a clear message instead of a quietly wrong graph. We also wrote automated tests for the statistics, that format check, and the question box.

What we found

Punjab: greener fields, and the rain doesn't explain it

Punjab is getting greener, and rain isn't the reason. Across the Indus plains, vegetation went up by about 0.028 per decade, which works out to around 13%, from 0.349 to 0.395. The odds of that being chance are under one in a thousand (p = 0.0007, with a range of 0.020 to 0.045). Rainfall over the same fields didn't trend at all (p = 0.43).

Indus plains: vegetation rising each year while rainfall stays flat

Wetter years are greener, with a correlation of 0.79, so rain explains the bumps from year to year. It just doesn't explain the long climb. The greening shows up in both seasons, including the dry winter, it picked up after 2018, and it survives when you take rain out of the picture. The most likely source is irrigation, and a lot of that is groundwater pumped up by tubewells. Green fields can hide falling water.

Warming passes the test on 72% of the planet

Globally, the warming is real. The planet has warmed about 0.21 C per decade since 1980, and 72% of it shows warming that passes the test even after correcting for chance. In our analysis Europe, the Arctic and the Mediterranean are warming roughly twice as fast as the average, and the global record stepped up after 2001.

And a lot of what looks like change on a map is noise. Twenty percent of the world's land looks like its vegetation changed when you test each place alone. After the correction it's six and a half.

What we want to add next

Groundwater from GRACE-FO is first. Our backend can already read it, we just haven't loaded the data yet. If the water under Punjab is falling while the fields get greener, that settles the irrigation question from space.

After that, the list is:

  • a monthly version of the trend test that can catch a change hiding in a single month, July monsoon rain for example
  • a heat measure based on how often a place breaks its own monthly record, which is closer to what people actually feel
  • a machine learning model that splits the greening between rain, heat and irrigation
  • local climate projections to 2100 from NASA's NEX-GDDP-CMIP6, to replace the global averages
  • VIIRS joined onto MODIS, so the vegetation record doesn't stop
  • proper district boundaries for Pakistan, so an agency can ask about exactly the area it manages

Why this matters to us

Pakistan is the third-largest user of groundwater in the world, after India and the United States. Almost three quarters of Punjab's farmland, about 76%, relies on groundwater at least partly, and Punjab grows most of the country's food. When those fields get greener without more rain, the water is coming out of the ground, and that can't go on forever.

EarthScope can show that from space, for free, long before the wells start running dry. The same approach works anywhere farming leans on groundwater, from the Indus to the North China Plain to the American High Plains. It also protects people from two opposite mistakes: panicking over one hot year, and brushing off a real trend as "just weather".

How it keeps going after the hackathon

The full plan is in our business model.

Free for everyone, paid where it saves money, and costs close to zero

The public site stays free for everyone, including every place, every record, every forecast and the downloads, and we don't plan to change that. Money would come from the organisations that save money or time with it:

  • Irrigation and agriculture departments would want trends for their own districts and canal areas, monthly reports, and an alert when a trend turns real.
  • Crop insurers and agricultural lenders could use verified vegetation and rainfall trends to price drought risk and decide on loans.
  • NGOs and development projects already budget for baselines and monitoring in their proposals and impact reports.
  • Newsrooms want a quick, citable way to check climate claims.

We'd offer three levels:

  • Public: the full site, free.
  • Analyst: adds API access, saved areas, PDF reports and an email when a trend becomes significant.
  • Institution: adds custom boundaries, extra data like GRACE-FO groundwater, monthly reports, training and support.

We'd also take on paid custom studies and apply for climate and innovation grants. We don't want to guess at prices, so the plan is to run three free pilots first, with a water or farming department, an NGO and a newsroom, and charge for whatever they actually found useful. Public bodies and nonprofits in Pakistan would get a discount.

Our costs are tiny, which is a big part of why we think this can last. NASA's data is free, and the website runs without a server. A typical visit downloads less than 1 MB, the free hosting plan handles thousands of visits a month, and 9 dollars a month would cover about 30,000. Almost anything we earn could go into people and new data instead of servers, and student and nonprofit cloud credits could cover the first year.

Hosting credits used against monthly visits, and what one visit downloads

The first year:

  • Months 1 to 3: go live properly, publish the Punjab result, add GRACE-FO, and share it with universities and newspapers in Pakistan.
  • Months 3 to 6: run the three pilots.
  • Months 6 to 9: turn the pilots into paid licences or grant-funded projects, and set real prices.
  • Months 9 to 12: add Pakistan's district boundaries, local projections to 2100, and the rest of South Asia.

Our first year: go live, pilots, first revenue, grow

Because every NASA record sits on the same global grid, the same pipeline works for any country that asks.

There are good tools out there already. NASA Worldview and Earthdata have an enormous catalogue of imagery, but they show you pictures, not a verdict. Google Earth Engine is powerful but meant for people who code. Global Forest Watch is excellent but focused on forests. Consultants can do this kind of work, but slowly and at a price most districts can't pay. We think the gap is a tested answer, in plain words, for any place, in a few seconds.

We know what could go wrong, too:

  • Someone could read a trend as proof of a cause, which is why every case says "consistent with".
  • MODIS will retire, so we're planning to join VIIRS onto it, and the backend can load any monthly grid with the same layout.
  • Government bodies often pay slowly, so we'd start with NGOs and grant-funded work and keep costs near zero.
  • People might trust the forecasts too much, so we only ever show ranges, with their real hit rate printed beside them.
  • If the site suddenly went viral, there's no server to crash. The only limit is the hosting allowance, and the paid plan covers about 30,000 visits a month.

What we'd measure is simple: how many agencies and NGOs use an EarthScope report in a real decision, how many districts we cover, how many pilots turn into funded work, how many of our findings get checked by university researchers, and how many climate claims get checked before they're printed. The work fits the UN's goals on zero hunger (2), clean water (6) and climate action (13).

How we built it, and our three days

The backend is Python, using FastAPI, xarray, NumPy and pandas, packaged with uv and Docker. It reads the NASA files, runs every test and forecast, and answers requests through a documented API. The website is plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with Apache ECharts for the charts and globe.gl and three.js for the globe and the 3D models.

One decision we're glad about is that the public site doesn't need a server at all. We ran our Python backend once over every map, every region, every 2 degree square on Earth and every forecast, and saved all the answers as files the website reads directly. That makes it fast, nearly free to run, and very hard to crash if lots of people show up at once. The live backend can still be switched on with one setting, and it gives identical answers because it's the same code. The site is hosted on Netlify under our own domain, earthscope.us, and the code is open source under the MIT licence.

How we spent the weekend, day by day and person by person

How the three days went:

  • Thursday: all five of us downloaded and cleaned the 36 GB of NASA data.
  • Friday, the long day: Muhammad Hadi led the frontend, Ibrahim built the backend, Ch Ahmed Mubashar and Mohammed Ahmed worked on the documents and charts, and Muhammad Shehroz led the research.
  • Saturday: we built the models and forecasts, joined the backend to the app, and finished the paper, the video and the presentation.

Everything we worked on is in the Proof of Work folder.

What we think makes it different

Most tools show you a chart and leave the conclusion to you. EarthScope tells you whether the change is real and how sure we are. It corrects its maps for luck, which a lot of climate maps don't. It found its main result by putting two records next to each other, and it can tell you when a change began and in which season, not just how big it is. Its forecasts show their own track record even where that record isn't great. Anyone can ask it a question in plain words, a few of them in Roman Urdu. The 3D scenes mean you don't need a statistics degree to understand how it works, and it runs without a server, so it's free and hard to break. Most of all, we pointed it at our own home and found something real about Pakistan's water.

Being honest about the limits

We show ranges instead of single lines, and we say "consistent with" instead of "caused by". Vegetation and rain only go back to 2010, which is short, so we don't claim anything about a rain trend. A 2 degree square is about 200 km across, so our results describe regions, not individual fields. Two trends moving together suggest a cause but don't prove one. Satellite rainfall is less reliable over snow, mountains and coastlines. The 3D scenes that are illustrations are labelled that way, and the real numbers always come from the app. EarthScope uses NASA data but isn't endorsed by NASA, and we don't use the NASA logo.

The team

The EarthScope team and what comes next

Everything described here runs on real NASA data. You can try it at earthscope.us/app, and the full method is in our research paper.
